procedural_history.impugned_order: Orders dated 15.11.2018 (rejecting the Final Report of the Investigating Officer and directing that the Protest Petition be registered as the Complaint Case) and 11.01.2022 (issuing summons to the respondents-accused) passed by the CJM.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Respondents-accused filed an application under Section 482 Cr.P.C. before the High Court challenging the order dated 11.01.2022. They then amended the application to also challenge the order dated 15.11.2018. The High Court allowed the amendment and then set aside both the orders dated 15.11.2018 and 11.01.2022, directing the Magistrate to pass a fresh order on the Protest Petition.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant-complainant approached the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's orders dated 21.07.2022 (allowing the amendment) and 22.07.2022 (setting aside the CJM's orders). The Supreme Court quashed and set aside the impugned orders passed by the High Court, and directed the concerned CJM to proceed with the complaint case in accordance with law.

directions: The impugned orders passed by the High Court being highly erroneous, the same are quashed and set aside.
The concerned CJM is directed to proceed with the complaint case in accordance with law.
It shall be open for the respondents-accused to respond to the summons and appear before the concerned CJM within two weeks.

issue.issue_text: Whether the course opted by the CJM in rejecting the final report submitted by the investigating officer and accepting the Protest Petition as a Complaint Case was just, legal and proper in the facts and circumstances of the case.

facts: After an investigation, the police submitted a final report.
The complainant, disagreeing with the report, filed a "Protest Petition".
The Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) rejected the police's final report and ordered that the Protest Petition be registered and treated as a formal Complaint Case.
The CJM then proceeded under Section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.), recorded statements from the complainant and eight witnesses, and issued summons to the accused.
The accused challenged the CJM's orders in the High Court, which set them aside.
The complainant then appealed the High Court's decision to the Supreme Court.
law: A Magistrate is not bound by the final report submitted by the police under Section 173 of the Cr.P.C.
When a final report is submitted, a Magistrate has the power and discretion to reject it and take cognizance of an offense based on a Protest Petition filed by the complainant.
Treating a Protest Petition as a complaint and proceeding under Section 200 Cr.P.C. is a legally valid option for the Magistrate.
application: The Supreme Court found that the CJM's decision to reject the police's final report and treat the Protest Petition as a complaint was a valid exercise of judicial discretion.
The Court explicitly stated that this course of action was "absolutely just, legal and proper in the facts and circumstances of the case."

The Court also noted a significant procedural flaw in the High Court's decision: the accused had waited nearly four years to challenge the CJM's initial order (from 2018) and only did so after summons were issued in 2022. The Supreme Court held that the High Court should not have allowed this delayed challenge or interfered with the CJM's lawful discretion.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the CJM acted correctly and within the law by rejecting the police's final report and treating the Protest Petition as a complaint case. The Court held that this action was just, legal, and proper, and therefore, it quashed the High Court's order and allowed the complaint case to proceed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the course opted by the CJM in rejecting the final report submitted by the investigating officer and accepting the Protest Petition as a Complaint Case was just, legal and proper in the facts and circumstances of the case.
appellant_arguments: The procedure adopted by the Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) was legally correct. The CJM was justified in rejecting the final report, treating the protest petition as a complaint, recording statements of the complainant and witnesses under Sections 200 and 202 Cr.P.C., and issuing summons upon finding a prima facie case. This course of action did not warrant interference by the High Court.
respondent_arguments: The CJM's order rejecting the final report and treating the protest petition as a complaint was improper. Consequently, the subsequent order issuing summons was also illegal and should be set aside.

cases.case_name: Rakesh & Another v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Another
cases.principle: When a police report is submitted, a Magistrate has three options: (1) drop the proceedings; (2) take cognizance under Section 190(1)(b) based on the police report, irrespective of the police's conclusion; or (3) take cognizance under Section 190(1)(a) based on the original complaint (or a protest petition) and follow the procedure under Sections 200 and 202. If the investigation is found to be unsatisfactory, the Magistrate should order further investigation before treating a protest petition as a complaint.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A Magistrate is not bound by the conclusion drawn by the police in a final report. Upon receipt of a police report, a Magistrate is empowered to take cognizance of an offence if satisfied that there is sufficient material on record. The Magistrate may: (1) accept the report and drop the proceedings; (2) take cognizance of the offence under Section 190(1)(b) based on the police report, without being bound by the police's conclusion; or (3) treat a protest petition as a complaint and take cognizance under Section 190(1)(a), proceeding to examine the complainant and witnesses under Section 200. This power to take cognizance on a complaint or protest petition exists even if the Magistrate has previously accepted the final report.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court found that the course of action taken by the Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) was entirely correct and legally sound. The CJM was well within his rights to reject the final report from the investigating officer, accept the protest petition as a formal complaint, proceed to record statements under the Criminal Procedure Code, and issue summons upon finding a prima facie case. Consequently, the High Court committed a gross error by interfering with the CJM's valid exercise of discretion and setting aside his orders.
legal_tests_applied: When a police report is submitted to a Magistrate, the Magistrate has several options, including: (1) dropping the action if there is no sufficient ground; (2) taking cognizance of the offence under Section 190(1)(b) based on the police report, irrespective of the police's conclusion; or (3) taking cognizance of the offence under Section 190(1)(a) based on the original complaint and proceeding to examine the complainant and witnesses under Sections 200 and 202 of the Cr.P.C.
why_appellant_lost: The High Court's observations, which led to the appellant losing in that court, were found to be 'absolutely erroneous' by the Supreme Court.

The High Court committed a 'gross error' by setting aside the CJM's orders, as the CJM's discretionary order to issue summons was based on recorded statements of nine people and a prima facie satisfaction of the crime, which did not warrant interference.
The High Court should not have permitted the respondents-accused to amend their application to challenge the CJM's initial order of 15.11.2018 after a delay of about four years.
why_respondent_won: The course opted by the CJM—rejecting the final report submitted by the Investigating Officer and accepting the Protest Petition to proceed further under Section 200 Cr.P.C.—was 'absolutely just, legal and proper in the facts and circumstances of the case.'

The CJM's order to issue summons on 11.01.2022 was a valid exercise of discretion, as it was done after recording the statements of the complainant and eight witnesses and after recording prima facie satisfaction about the commission of the alleged crime.
policy_considerations: A higher court should not interfere with a lower court's valid exercise of discretion when it is exercised within the four corners of the law.

Challenges to judicial orders should not be permitted after a significant and unexplained delay, as the High Court should not have allowed the challenge to a 2018 order to be added by amendment in 2022.
